analysis.one_liner: Extends government health coverage for low-income children through 2013, funded by higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: The children's health insurance reauthorization passed the House 289-139 and the Senate 66-32, and the president signed it into law on February 4, 2009 as Public Law 111-3.
analysis.plain_summary: This law extends and expands the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), the joint federal-state program covering children in families that earn too much for Medicaid but cannot afford private coverage. It renews funding through fiscal year 2013 at higher levels, lets states cover low-income pregnant women and simplify enrollment, requires dental coverage and mental health parity, and pays for it by raising federal excise taxes on tobacco products. It also narrows the program's reach: coverage for childless adults is phased out, federal funds cannot pay for people not lawfully in the country, and states get less federal help if they cover children in families above 300% of the poverty line.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income children who are eligible for CHIP or Medicaid but not enrolled, and in states that choose to, low-income pregnant women and newborns automatically enrolled at birth. The bill states its purpose is to enroll all six million uninsured children who are eligible but not signed up. Families also gain required dental coverage, mental health parity, a 30-day grace period before coverage can be cut off, and a simpler citizenship-verification process that replaces a paperwork-heavy documentation rule.

how_it_helps.text: Reauthorizes CHIP through fiscal year 2013 at increased levels, with roughly $33 billion a year allocated by FY2012 (about $15 billion annually), and states it aims to enroll all six million eligible but uninsured children.
Gives states the option to cover targeted low-income pregnant women through CHIP and automatically enrolls children born to women receiving such assistance for their first year of life.
Requires CHIP coverage of necessary dental services, mental health parity with medical and surgical benefits, and a 30-day grace period before coverage can be terminated for nonpayment.

Lets states verify citizenship with a name and Social Security number instead of documentation, and permits states to waive the five-year waiting period before lawfully residing immigrant children and pregnant women can receive coverage.

Funds outreach and enrollment grants, a national enrollment campaign, and an 'Express Lane' option letting states use other agencies' data to simplify eligibility determinations, and pays states performance bonuses for reducing the number of uninsured low-income children.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco consumers and the tobacco industry, through higher federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless and pipe tobacco, plus a tax on stocked (floor-stocks) tobacco inventories. There is also a small shift of corporate estimated tax payments: a 0.5% increase in installments due in mid-2013, which accelerates revenue into an earlier fiscal year without raising the total owed.

drawbacks.text: The higher excise taxes fall on tobacco users, and because smoking is more common among lower-income people, the financing weighs hardest on some of the same households the program serves.
The law phases out CHIP coverage for nonpregnant childless adults after 2009, ending an existing use of CHIP funds for adults in some states.

Federal funding is denied for individuals not lawfully residing in the United States, and states covering children with family income above 300% of the poverty line receive the lower Medicaid matching rate rather than the enhanced CHIP rate.

The law expands a state option to route CHIP and Medicaid dollars to families who have access to employer-sponsored coverage as premium assistance, and it requires employer group health plans to open special enrollment periods for people leaving Medicaid or CHIP — embedding private insurance in the program's structure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear: expanded coverage for low-income children, dental and mental health guarantees, and easier enrollment, financed mainly by a tobacco tax whose burden lands disproportionately on low-income smokers and the tobacco industry. The childless-adult phase-out and the 300% income limit pull the bill back toward the program's original child focus rather than broad public coverage. On balance the law's benefits to children are large and direct, and its financing offsets them with a real, regressive cost.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 289-139, the Senate amended it and passed 66-32, the House accepted the Senate's version 290-135, and the president signed it the same day.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 289-139 on January 14, 2009, a day after rejecting 179-247 a motion to recommit offered by Rep. Nathan Deal that sought changes to how CHIP funds are used.
The Senate passed it with an amendment 66-32 on January 29, 2009, and appointed conferees Baucus, Rockefeller, Conrad, Grassley, and Hatch.
The House agreed to the Senate amendment 290-135 on February 4, 2009, and the president signed it that day as Public Law 111-3.

The final law differs from the bill as introduced: it adds a new Medicaid and CHIP advisory commission (MACPAC), a dental-only supplemental option, and it reduced the mid-2013 corporate estimated tax shift from 1% to 0.5%.

The bill as introduced had also prohibited new physician ownership or investment in hospitals and hospital capacity expansion; that provision is not among the sections of the enacted law, whose final titles run only through the tobacco revenue provisions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-income children, pregnant women, and their families gained coverage and benefit guarantees. Private insurers and employer plans had their role preserved through the premium-assistance option and special enrollment requirements. Tobacco companies absorbed higher excise taxes, and tobacco users paid more.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats backed it nearly unanimously (249 of 255 in the House, 55 of 56 in the Senate) while most Republicans opposed it (137 of 178 House Republicans and 32 of 41 Senate Republicans voted no).

industries.note: The law raises federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, and roll-your-own tobacco, taxes floor-stocked inventories, and expands Treasury's power over tobacco permits. It also carves out certain cigars and cigarette papers from the floor-stocks tax and adds a $500 credit, a partial cushion for some in the trade.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The law builds CHIP around private coverage: states may use federal CHIP and Medicaid dollars to pay premiums for employer-sponsored plans, employer group health plans must open special enrollment periods for families moving between Medicaid/CHIP and job-based coverage, and a Senate statement in the law affirms 'building upon the existing private health insurance market.' Managed care entities also face Medicaid-style quality safeguards, but their channel role in serving CHIP families is locked in.

industries.industry: Federally qualified health centers and rural health clinics
industries.note: The law applies the Medicare prospective payment system to services these safety-net clinics provide, which standardizes their payment. It simultaneously boosts enrollment of the low-income patients they serve.
